responses.reason: R2 credits the zero-based grouped bars, the 0-100% axis and the disclosed 0.5 pp threshold, all of which are sound. I keep 3 because the analysis declares on-time rate the primary metric yet the trend defaults to Order volume and offers no change-from-baseline view, so the delivered design is slightly at odds with its own hierarchy. R2's evidence does not address that default.

The insight band, three KPI cards and trend/outcome row form a clear path, but the fixed prototype pill covers the 'Delivered on time' row and the outcomes card carries a large dead area beneath its footnote. R2 calls this the strongest composition of the three pairs; I see a strong composition with two visible blemishes, so 3 rather than 4.

R2 lists the same defects (604px mobile document, 22 contrast nodes, overlay over content) but still scores 3. A shipped mobile page that overflows by 214px with a region table clipped mid-column and no visible scroll hint, plus extensive contrast failures, is not a fully working result; 2 reflects that while acknowledging the code is coherent and error-free.

R2's crop shows the region table caption 'Lowest rate first' while rows render Central 95.4%, East 92.4%, North 91.0%, South 91.3%, West 89.4% in fixed order. I missed that the promised ranking is not applied; the correctly ranked 'Largest regional declines' panel partly compensates, but the table's scan order is wrong, so 3 is correct.

R2 identifies the half-empty chart row as a conspicuous composition failure. I agree it is conspicuous and already scored it down from excellent, but the headline, rate-first card row and section order remain clear and scannable; one broken row does not make the hierarchy merely adequate, so I keep 3.

R2 folds the unsorted table and the broken grid into this dimension, but both are layout/correctness defects, not missing states or feedback. Loading, stale, partial, error, no-data, empty result, no-denominator and in-progress variants are all implemented, the orders view keeps search/paging/sorting and drill chips; the interaction set is complete, so I keep 4.

R2 scores 2 for two contrast nodes and four label/name mismatches, but also records no page-level overflow and all 40 controls named. Candidate A in this pair has 22 contrast nodes plus a 604px document and I scored it 1; B's findings are real but much narrower, so 3 preserves that measured gap.

R2's source-level finding changes my judgment: a stray closing div in chartSVG (app.js:850) closes the 12-column grid after the chart, so the status, region and decline cards escape the intended layout. Combined with the unimplemented region sort, that is a structural markup bug rather than a styling nit; 2 is right.

differences_remaining: design_judgment, candidate A: I keep 3 against R2's 4 because the default trend shows volume despite on-time rate being declared primary, and no change view is offered.
visual_hierarchy, candidate A: I keep 3 against R2's 4 because the prototype pill covers an outcome row and the outcomes card leaves dead space.
implementation_quality, candidate A: I keep 2 against R2's 3 because the 604px mobile document, clipped table and 22 contrast nodes are shipped defects.
visual_hierarchy, candidate B: I keep 3 against R2's 2 because the rest of the hierarchy is strong despite the half-empty chart row.
interaction_completeness, candidate B: I keep 4 against R2's 3 because the sort and grid problems are layout defects, not missing interaction states.
accessibility_responsiveness, candidate B: I keep 3 against R2's 2 because there is no page overflow and the findings are far narrower than candidate A's.
summary: I revised Candidate B's ux_reasoning and implementation_quality after the counterpart identified the unsorted region table and the stray closing div that breaks the 12-column grid, which narrows B's lead to 3.35 against 3.20. The other six positional disputes were maintained, mostly weighting the same measured defects differently.
